# Executive Summary {.unnumbered}

Every country that taxes carbon believes it is pricing emissions. Most of them are
measuring the wrong thing. The wrong thing is the nominal rate. The right thing is
the price the economy actually feels.

A \$30 carbon tax applied to a fuel that nobody can substitute away from is a revenue
instrument. The same tax applied to a fuel with a clean alternative is a transition
instrument. The number is the same. The effect on emissions is not. The Total
Effective Carbon Price measures what the economy feels.

## The headline formula {.unnumbered}

$$
\tau^{*} \;=\; \frac{1}{\Lambda}\;\sum_{s}\sum_{f} E_{fs}\;\Big[\;
\tilde{\varepsilon}^{\,\mathrm{int}}_{fs} \cdot \tau^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs}
\;+\;
\tilde{\varepsilon}^{\,\mathrm{ext}}_{s} \cdot \tau^{\mathrm{ext}}_{s}
\;\Big]
$$ {#eq-tecp}

Each fuel's emissions $E_{fs}$ are multiplied by two terms. The first is an
intensive (fuel-switching) semi-elasticity $\tilde{\varepsilon}^{\,\mathrm{int}}$
times the intensive component of the policy price. The second is an extensive
(demand-reduction) semi-elasticity $\tilde{\varepsilon}^{\,\mathrm{ext}}$ times the
extensive component. $\Lambda$ is a normalisation constant: what a \$1/tCO~2~
uniform carbon tax would achieve in this economy.

## Why it matters {.unnumbered}

- Two countries can have identical nominal carbon prices and very different TECPs.
  A country with few substitution alternatives but high demand elasticity will
  price emissions effectively through the extensive margin. A country with abundant
  substitutes but inelastic demand will price effectively through the intensive
  margin.
- A country with no carbon tax at all can have a meaningful TECP if its feebates,
  fuel duties, and clean fuel standards create sufficient price separation between
  dirty and clean fuels.
- Existing metrics — the OECD's Effective Carbon Rate, the IMF's effective carbon
  price — add up sticker prices. They cannot answer the question a finance minister
  actually needs answered: *if I replaced my entire policy package with a single
  uniform carbon tax, what rate would deliver the same emissions reduction?*

## The microeconomic engine {.unnumbered}

The TECP requires a demand model. The model must do three things. It must handle
multiple fuels competing within a sector. It must distinguish using less energy
from switching to a different energy source. And it must handle the fact that
switching takes longer than conserving.

A nested constant-elasticity-of-substitution (CES) structure does all three. Within
each sector, fuels substitute against each other with elasticity $\sigma$. Across
sectors, total energy demand responds to the aggregate energy price with
elasticity $\eta$. A partial adjustment mechanism with separate speeds for the two
margins captures the fact that conservation can be immediate while fuel switching
requires capital replacement.

The CES is the right level of structure for this task. It is rich enough to
distinguish the two margins and to generate the elasticity matrix consistently
from a small number of parameters. It is simple enough to calibrate from published
estimates and to compute on a spreadsheet. Where it falls short — notably, it
imposes a constant substitution elasticity across the price range — the error is
small for the policy ranges of interest, and the framework can be extended to
higher nests if needed.

# Part I — The Total Effective Carbon Price {.unnumbered}

# Motivation

## The problem with existing metrics

Climate policy is heterogeneous by design. A finance minister facing a binding
emissions target and an unhappy electorate does not choose a single instrument;
she chooses a package. The package may include a carbon tax on industry, a feebate
on vehicles, an emissions trading system covering power, a clean fuel standard for
transport, fuel excise duties, and possibly subsidies for renewable energy. Each
instrument has different distributional, political-economy, and competitiveness
implications. Each works through different channels. Comparing two countries'
climate policy ambition therefore requires comparing two packages, not two numbers.

Existing metrics duck this problem. The OECD's Effective Carbon Rate sums explicit
carbon prices, ETS prices, and fuel excise duties into a single nominal rate. The
IMF's effective carbon price does much the same. Both are useful because they
aggregate visible price signals across instruments and across fuels. But they
aggregate by addition, weighted only by emissions — not by the responsiveness of
those emissions to each instrument. A dollar of fuel duty on diesel (where
alternatives are scarce in the short run) is treated identically to a dollar of
fuel duty on petrol (where switching is easier). A feebate — which contains no
explicit carbon price at all but creates a wedge between clean and dirty
alternatives — contributes zero. A clean fuel standard (which forces a switch
through a quantity instrument) contributes zero. This is the wrong answer.

## What the TECP measures

The TECP asks a different question: *what uniform carbon tax $\tau^{*}$ would deliver
the same total emissions reduction as the actual policy package?* The answer is a
single number, in \$/tCO~2~, that makes any heterogeneous package comparable to any
other and to a hypothetical uniform tax. It admits feebates, fuel standards, and
renewable mandates on equal terms with explicit carbon prices, because the
comparison is in emissions reduced, not in price imposed.

Critically, the TECP is decomposable. The same single number can be opened up to
show which margin is doing the work (intensive versus extensive) and which sector
is contributing what (transport, industry, power, buildings). This makes it
diagnostically useful, not just headline-useful.

# Notation and setup

The economy has sectors $s$ and fuels $f$. The key quantities are:

- $E_{fs}$: baseline CO~2~ emissions from fuel $f$ in sector $s$ (tCO~2~).
- $p_{fs}$: market price of fuel $f$ delivered to sector $s$, in \$/PJ of final energy.
- $e_{fs}$: emission factor for fuel $f$ in sector $s$, in tCO~2~/PJ.
- $\varphi_{fs}$: technical efficiency — the share of input fuel energy that becomes useful service.
- $\sigma_s$: within-sector elasticity of substitution among fuels.
- $\eta_s$: own-price elasticity of aggregate service demand for sector $s$.

## Technical efficiency $\varphi$

The same physical unit of fuel does not deliver the same service. An electric
motor converts roughly 85% of input electricity into mechanical work; an internal
combustion engine roughly 25%; a gas-fired condensing boiler roughly 90%; a CCGT
power plant roughly 50%. The CES operates over *useful service*, not over input
energy. The framework therefore tracks effective prices $\tilde{p} = p/\varphi$ and
effective emission factors $\tilde{e} = e/\varphi$. This is what makes
electrification look like substitution rather than expansion: a kilowatt-hour of
electricity used in a vehicle delivers more service than a kilowatt-hour of petrol,
and the model sees that.

# Semi-elasticities and policy decomposition

## From CES to semi-elasticities

The CES (developed in detail in Part II) generates an elasticity matrix from
$\sigma$ and the service shares $\hat{w}$. For fuel $f$ in sector $s$:

$$
\varepsilon^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs} = -\sigma_s \,(1 - \hat{w}_{fs}),
\qquad
\varepsilon^{\mathrm{ext}}_{s} = -\eta_s
$$ {#eq-ces-isoelastic}

The intensive elasticity is the within-sector substitution effect: a higher price
for fuel $f$ moves the mix away from $f$, scaled by how dominant $f$ is in the
current mix. The extensive elasticity is the cross-sectoral demand response: a
higher aggregate energy price moves total service demand down. Both are isoelastic;
to use them in a TECP formula we convert to **semi-elasticities** by dividing by
the price level $\tilde{p}_{fs} = p_{fs}/\varphi_{fs}$:

$$
\tilde{\varepsilon}^{\,\mathrm{int}}_{fs} = \varepsilon^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs} \, / \, \tilde{p}_{fs},
\qquad
\tilde{\varepsilon}^{\,\mathrm{ext}}_{s} = \varepsilon^{\mathrm{ext}}_{s} \, / \, \tilde{p}_{s}
$$ {#eq-semi-elasticities}

Semi-elasticities tell us the absolute change in quantity per dollar change in
price, rather than the percentage change per percentage change. They are the
natural objects for combining with policy prices stated in \$/tCO~2~.

## Decomposing the policy price

Every policy instrument creates two kinds of price signals. It raises the cost of
using a particular fuel (intensive signal: $\tau^{\mathrm{int}}$). And it raises the
average cost of energy services, which reduces total service demand (extensive
signal: $\tau^{\mathrm{ext}}$). For most instruments these two signals are bundled.

To take the cases that matter:

- A **uniform carbon tax** $\tau$ at \$X/tCO~2~ produces
  $\tau^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs} = X \cdot (e_{fs} - \bar{e}_s)$ and
  $\tau^{\mathrm{ext}}_{s} = X \cdot \bar{e}_s$, where $\bar{e}_s$ is the
  energy-share-weighted mean emission factor in sector $s$. The intensive
  component is the within-sector wedge; the extensive component is the common cost
  increase.
- A **feebate** is a pure intensive instrument: it imposes
  $\tau^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs} = X \cdot (e_{fs} - \bar{e}_s)$ and
  $\tau^{\mathrm{ext}}_{s} = 0$. By construction it leaves the average sector cost
  unchanged.
- A **fuel excise duty** is closer to a pure extensive instrument when applied
  uniformly across all fuels in a sector, but typically applies only to a subset
  of fuels and so generates both signals.
- A **clean fuel standard** (a quantity instrument) is dual to a feebate: it
  generates an intensive wedge equal to the shadow price of the standard. The
  extensive component is small and follows from the average abatement cost.

# The TECP formula

## Derivation

Total emissions reduction from a policy package is the sum over fuels and sectors
of intensive plus extensive effects. The intensive effect in sector $s$ is
$\tilde{\varepsilon}^{\,\mathrm{int}}_{fs} \cdot \tau^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs}$ (units:
t/PJ). The extensive effect in sector $s$ is
$\tilde{\varepsilon}^{\,\mathrm{ext}}_{s} \cdot \tau^{\mathrm{ext}}_{s}$. Weighting
by baseline emissions $E_{fs}$ and summing:

$$
\Delta\text{Emissions}
=
\sum_{s}\sum_{f} E_{fs} \cdot
\big[\; \tilde{\varepsilon}^{\,\mathrm{int}}_{fs} \cdot \tau^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs}
\;+\; \tilde{\varepsilon}^{\,\mathrm{ext}}_{s} \cdot \tau^{\mathrm{ext}}_{s} \;\big]
$$ {#eq-emissions}

Setting this equal to the emissions reduction from a counterfactual uniform carbon
tax $\tau^{*}$, and solving for $\tau^{*}$, gives the headline formula
(@eq-tecp), where the normalisation constant $\Lambda$ is the abatement that a
\$1/tCO~2~ uniform tax would generate. Algebraically:

$$
\Lambda \;=\; \sum_{s}\sum_{f} E_{fs} \cdot
\big[\; \tilde{\varepsilon}^{\,\mathrm{int}}_{fs} \cdot (e_{fs} - \bar{e}_s)
\;+\; \tilde{\varepsilon}^{\,\mathrm{ext}}_{s} \cdot \bar{e}_s \;\big]
$$ {#eq-lambda}

## The role of the $\Omega$ weights

Rearranging the formula reveals the abatement weights. For each fuel-sector cell
define:

$$
\Omega^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs} = \frac{E_{fs} \cdot \tilde{\varepsilon}^{\,\mathrm{int}}_{fs}}{\Lambda},
\qquad
\Omega^{\mathrm{ext}}_{s} = \frac{\big(\sum_{f} E_{fs}\big) \cdot \tilde{\varepsilon}^{\,\mathrm{ext}}_{s}}{\Lambda}
$$ {#eq-omega}

These weights are properties of the economy, not of the policy. They are computed
once from the energy balance, fuel prices, emission factors, and demand
elasticities. After that, evaluating any policy scenario is a single weighted sum:

$$
\tau^{*} \;=\; \sum_{s}\sum_{f} \Omega^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs} \cdot \tau^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs}
\;+\; \sum_{s} \Omega^{\mathrm{ext}}_{s} \cdot \tau^{\mathrm{ext}}_{s}
$$ {#eq-tecp-omega}

This is the framework's key operational property. The policy enters only through
the instrument-specific effective prices on each margin. Change the policy,
recompute the TECP in milliseconds. No re-solving of equilibrium, no re-running of
models.

# Decomposition and diagnostics

## By margin

The TECP decomposes additively into intensive and extensive contributions:
$\tau^{*} = \tau^{*}_{\mathrm{int}} + \tau^{*}_{\mathrm{ext}}$. A feebate
contributes only to $\tau^{*}_{\mathrm{int}}$. A pure quantity-side demand reduction
(e.g. a road pricing scheme that does not vary by fuel) contributes only to
$\tau^{*}_{\mathrm{ext}}$. A carbon tax contributes to both, in proportions that
depend on the sector's emission-factor variance.

## By sector

The TECP further decomposes by sector: $\tau^{*} = \sum_{s} \tau^{*}_{s}$. This
reveals where each instrument is doing the work. A carbon tax on industrial fuels
may contribute heavily to $\tau^{*}$ in industry and negligibly elsewhere. A
vehicle feebate contributes only to transport. Aggregating across instruments by
sector tells the policymaker which sectors are over- or under-priced relative to
their baseline emissions.

## Special cases

Three special cases anchor intuition. First, if all policies are removed,
$\tau^{*} = 0$. Second, if the only policy is a uniform carbon tax at rate $X$,
then $\tau^{*} = X$ exactly. Third, if the policy package is a sequence of
overlapping instruments (e.g. a carbon tax plus a feebate), $\tau^{*}$ is the sum
of the carbon-tax-equivalents of each instrument.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Part II — CES Energy Demand and Partial Adjustment {.unnumbered}

# The demand model

## What the model must do

The TECP requires a demand model underneath it. By "demand model" we mean
something specific: a structure that translates "this policy changes the price of
fuel X by Y" into "this is how much emissions fall, and through which channel."
The model must do three things. It must handle multiple fuels competing within a
sector. It must distinguish using less energy from switching to a different
energy source. And it must handle the fact that these responses take time.

## Why CES

A nested constant-elasticity-of-substitution (CES) structure does all three. At
the lower nest, fuels within a sector substitute against each other with
elasticity $\sigma$. This captures the intensive margin — the degree to which a
price change on one fuel causes the economy to shift toward another. At the upper
nest, aggregate energy demand responds to the overall energy price with elasticity
$\eta$, capturing the extensive margin. The two nests interact: a carbon tax
raises the price of dirty fuels, which both reduces total energy demand (upper
nest) and shifts the fuel mix toward cleaner alternatives (lower nest). The
relative strength of these two effects depends on the elasticities, which vary by
sector and country.

## Functional form

Within sector $s$, useful service $Q_s$ is produced from fuels indexed by $f$ via
the CES aggregator:

$$
Q_s \;=\; \left[\; \sum_{f} \alpha_{fs}^{\,1/\sigma_s}
\cdot (\varphi_{fs} \cdot q_{fs})^{(\sigma_s - 1)/\sigma_s} \right]^{\sigma_s/(\sigma_s - 1)}
$$ {#eq-ces-aggregator}

where $q_{fs}$ is physical input of fuel $f$, $\varphi_{fs}$ the technical
conversion efficiency to useful service, and $\alpha_{fs}$ the share parameter
calibrated from base-year energy shares. Cost minimisation yields fuel demand:

$$
q_{fs} \;=\; Q_s \cdot (\alpha_{fs} / \varphi_{fs})
\cdot (\tilde{p}_{fs} / C_s)^{-\sigma_s}
$$ {#eq-fuel-demand}

where $\tilde{p}_{fs} = p_{fs}/\varphi_{fs}$ is the effective price (per unit of
useful service) and $C_s$ is the CES unit cost index. At the upper nest, service
demand responds to $C_s$ with elasticity $\eta$:

$$
Q_s \;=\; \bar{Q}_s \cdot (C_s / \bar{C}_s)^{-\eta_s}
$$ {#eq-upper-nest}

# Local equivalence with isoelastic demand

## The relationship

A CES is isoelastic in a specific sense. The substitution elasticity is constant
by construction, and if paired with a constant-elasticity demand at the upper
nest, the system is isoelastic in its component elasticities. The composite
emissions response to a carbon price is not exactly isoelastic — because a uniform
carbon tax adds $\tau \cdot e_{fs}$ to each fuel, a larger percentage increase for
cheap high-carbon fuels than for expensive low-carbon ones — but the decomposition
into intensive and extensive channels is approximately isoelastic over a useful
range.

## The conversion chain

For any base point, CES → isoelastic → semi-elasticity is a sequence of local
linearisations:

- **Step 1.** From CES: $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{intensive}} = -\sigma \cdot (1 - \hat{w})$,
  where $\hat{w}$ is the service share. $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{extensive}} = -\eta$.
- **Step 2.** From isoelastic: at the base point, semi-elasticities
  $\tilde{\varepsilon} = \varepsilon / \tilde{p}$.
- **Step 3.** Use semi-elasticities to combine policy prices in
  \$/tCO~2~ × emission factor units.

The linearisation error is small when individual fuel price changes are under
roughly 20% of base price, which covers most realistic carbon prices and feebate
rates. For large perturbations a bisection over CES iterations is preferable, but
for cross-country comparison the linear scaling is standard and defensible.

# Partial adjustment

## Why adjustment takes time

Energy demand does not respond to price changes instantaneously. Conservation —
turning down a thermostat, driving fewer miles — can happen quickly because it
requires only behavioural change. Fuel switching — replacing a petrol vehicle with
an electric one, replacing a gas boiler with a heat pump — requires capital
investment and therefore replacement cycles. A carbon tax announced today changes
behaviour within months and changes capital stocks over decades.

## The split-speed model

The framework therefore distinguishes adjustment speeds by margin. Let
$\lambda^{\mathrm{int}}$ be the per-period adjustment rate on the intensive margin
and $\lambda^{\mathrm{ext}}$ on the extensive margin. The actual response in
period $t$ to a shock at time 0 is:

$$
\frac{\Delta q_t}{q_0}
\;=\; \big(1 - e^{-\lambda^{\mathrm{int}} t}\big) \cdot \varepsilon^{\mathrm{int}}_{\mathrm{LR}} \cdot \frac{\Delta p}{p}
\;+\; \big(1 - e^{-\lambda^{\mathrm{ext}} t}\big) \cdot \varepsilon^{\mathrm{ext}}_{\mathrm{LR}} \cdot \frac{\Delta C}{C}
$$ {#eq-partial-adjustment}

Empirical estimates put $\lambda^{\mathrm{int}}$ near 0.5–1.0 per year (so most of
the conservation response is in within two years) and $\lambda^{\mathrm{ext}}$
near 0.05–0.10 (so capital switching plays out over 10–20 years). The TECP can be
computed at any horizon; long-run TECP uses the long-run elasticities, short-run
TECP uses the appropriately scaled fraction. For policy analysis the long-run
TECP is the natural reference point because it tells the policymaker what the
package will eventually deliver if maintained.

# Calibration

## Substitution elasticities

Calibration uses published elasticity estimates. The literature converges on
plausible ranges by sector:

| Sector              | $\sigma$ (substitution) | $\eta$ (own-price demand) |
|---------------------|-------------------------|---------------------------|
| Road transport      | 1.0 – 1.5               | −0.3 to −0.6              |
| Power generation    | 2.0 – 4.0               | −0.2 to −0.5              |
| Residential heating | 1.0 – 2.0               | −0.3 to −0.5              |
| Industry (non-power)| 0.5 – 1.5               | −0.2 to −0.4              |

: Sector-level CES parameter ranges from the empirical literature {#tbl-calibration}

These ranges are long-run estimates from meta-analyses of fuel demand studies
[@stern2012; @labandeira2017]. Power generation has the highest $\sigma$ because
at the margin the dispatch decision is responsive to fuel prices, subject to
capacity constraints. Road transport has lower $\sigma$ because switching
requires vehicle replacement; $\sigma$ rises over longer horizons.

## Capital intensity and the behavioural interpretation of $\sigma$

A natural objection: technologies have very different capital intensities (an EV
is more capital-intensive than an ICE car, a heat pump than a gas boiler), and a
pure energy-CES does not see capital. Does this matter?

It matters, but less than one might think, because $\sigma$ is a behavioural
parameter rather than a physical one. The empirical $\sigma$ for road transport
at, say, 1.5 already reflects the fact that switching from petrol to electricity
requires buying a new car. The calibrated value of $\sigma$ is the *observed*
responsiveness of fuel quantities to relative fuel prices, integrated over the
relevant horizon and over the relevant capital stock. For the purposes of TECP —
comparing the abatement effectiveness of policies at the margin — this is
adequate. A more refined treatment would model capital explicitly through a
putty-clay structure; the cost in complexity is not justified for a metric whose
primary use is cross-country comparison.

# Implementation

## Computation

A complete TECP calculation requires:

1. baseline energy balance by sector and fuel;
2. market prices, emission factors and technical efficiencies;
3. sector-specific $\sigma$ and $\eta$;
4. policy parameters mapped to intensive and extensive carbon prices on each
   fuel-sector cell.

The computation has three steps: compute the $\Omega$ weights once; map each
policy to its intensive and extensive components; take the weighted sum. The
prototype runs in Excel in under a second per scenario.

## Spreadsheet layout

A practical layout has one row per fuel-sector cell. Columns hold: emissions,
service share, effective emission factor and sector mean, effective price and
CES cost index, isoelastic elasticities, semi-elasticities, intensive and
extensive policy prices, and $\Omega$ weights. The TECP is a single
`SUMPRODUCT`. Decomposition by margin and by sector is reading off totals from
row groupings.

## Worked example

A simple illustrative case: a country with a \$50/tCO~2~ economy-wide carbon tax,
a vehicle feebate delivering an effective intensive price equivalent to
\$35/tCO~2~ in road transport, and fuel excise duties contributing the equivalent
of \$15/tCO~2~ economy-wide. The TECP is roughly \$75/tCO~2~ — not \$100, because
the feebate operates only in transport (one of several sectors) and only on the
intensive margin. The ratio of \$75/\$50 = 1.5 tells the policymaker that the
non-tax instruments are adding about 50% to the effective carbon price beyond the
explicit tax.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Conclusions and uses

## What the metric does

The TECP turns climate policy comparison from a debate about instrument types
into a calculation with a single number. It can be applied to a country, a region,
or the world. It can be computed as a snapshot or projected forward as a
trajectory. It admits any combination of instruments and weights them by what
they actually do, not by what they nominally cost.

## What it does not do

The TECP is a marginal abatement metric, not a welfare metric. It does not
capture distributional consequences, fiscal revenue, leakage, or political
durability. A policy with a high TECP may still be a bad policy. The TECP answers
"how much abatement does this package deliver?", not "is this package good?" —
and the two are not the same question.

## Where the metric is most useful

- **Cross-country climate ambition comparison.** The TECP is the right
  denominator: not nominal carbon prices, but effective carbon prices weighted by
  abatement responsiveness.
- **Diagnostic decomposition.** Which margin is doing the work? Which sector is
  over- or under-priced? The TECP decomposes additively along both dimensions.
- **Counterfactual policy design.** Replacing a feebate with a carbon tax of
  equivalent TECP is a first-order welfare-neutral move. The TECP is the right
  exchange rate.
- **Trajectory planning.** Computed annually, the TECP gives a single trajectory
  for the effective climate price signal in the economy, against which any
  package can be benchmarked.

# Appendix: Complete Formula Reference {.appendix .unnumbered}

Throughout: fuel $f$ in sector $s$, year $t$. Baseline (year 0) quantities
$q^{0}_{fs}$, prices $p^{0}_{fs}$, emission factors $e_f$. CES substitution
elasticity $\sigma_s$, demand elasticity $\eta_s$.

## A.1  CES cost index {.unnumbered}

$$
C_{s,t} \;=\; \left(\sum_{f} \alpha_{fs}\; p_{fs,t}^{\,1-\sigma_s}\right)^{1/(1-\sigma_s)}
$$

where $\alpha_{fs}$ are calibrated share parameters from the base year.

## A.2  CES equilibrium quantities {.unnumbered}

$$
q^{*}_{fs,t} \;=\; q_{fs,t-1}
\left(\frac{p_{fs,t}}{p_{fs,t-1}}\right)^{-\sigma_s}
\left(\frac{C_{s,t}}{C_{s,t-1}}\right)^{\sigma_s + \eta_s}
$$

## A.3  Isoelastic equilibrium quantities {.unnumbered}

$$
q^{*}_{fs,t} \;=\; q_{fs,t-1}
\prod_{g} \left(\frac{p_{gs,t}}{p_{gs,t-1}}\right)^{\varepsilon_{fg,s}}
$$

## A.4  Partial adjustment (single speed) {.unnumbered}

$$
q_{fs,t} \;=\; q_{fs,t-1} \;+\; \lambda_s \big(q^{*}_{fs,t} - q_{fs,t-1}\big)
$$

## A.5  Partial adjustment (split speeds) {.unnumbered}

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q_{s,t}   &\;=\; Q_{s,t-1} + \lambda^{\mathrm{ext}}_{s}\,\big(Q^{*}_{s,t} - Q_{s,t-1}\big) \\
w_{fs,t}  &\;=\; w_{fs,t-1} + \lambda^{\mathrm{int}}_{s}\,\big(w^{*}_{fs,t} - w_{fs,t-1}\big) \\
q_{fs,t}  &\;=\; w_{fs,t} \cdot Q_{s,t}
\end{aligned}
$$

## A.6  Elasticity matrix from CES {.unnumbered}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\varepsilon_{ff,s} &\;=\; -\sigma_s + (\sigma_s + \eta_s)\,s_{fs} \\
\varepsilon_{fg,s} &\;=\; (\sigma_s + \eta_s)\,s_{gs} \qquad (g \neq f)
\end{aligned}
$$

## A.7  Semi-elasticities from CES {.unnumbered}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tilde{\varepsilon}^{\,\mathrm{int}}_{fs}
&\;=\; \sigma_s\,(1 - w_{fs})\;\frac{e_f - \bar{e}_s}{p_{fs}} \\[4pt]
\tilde{\varepsilon}^{\,\mathrm{ext}}_{s}
&\;=\; |\eta_s|\;\frac{\bar{e}_s}{C_s}
\end{aligned}
$$

## A.8  Adjustment speed from empirical elasticities {.unnumbered}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lambda &\;\approx\; \sigma^{\mathrm{SR}} \,/\, \sigma^{\mathrm{LR}} \\
\sigma  &\;=\; \sigma^{\mathrm{LR}} \\
\sigma^{\mathrm{eff}}_{T} &\;=\; \sigma\big[1 - (1 - \lambda)^{T}\big] \\
t_{1/2} &\;=\; \ln 2 \,/\, \ln\!\big(1/(1 - \lambda)\big) \;\approx\; \ln 2 \,/\, \lambda
\end{aligned}
$$

## A.9  Headline TECP formula {.unnumbered}

$$
\tau^{*} \;=\; \frac{1}{\Lambda}\;\sum_{s}\sum_{f} E_{fs}
\Big[\; \tilde{\varepsilon}^{\,\mathrm{int}}_{fs} \cdot \tau^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs}
\;+\; \tilde{\varepsilon}^{\,\mathrm{ext}}_{s} \cdot \tau^{\mathrm{ext}}_{s} \;\Big]
$$

with normalisation

$$
\Lambda \;=\; \sum_{s}\sum_{f} E_{fs}
\Big[\; \tilde{\varepsilon}^{\,\mathrm{int}}_{fs} \cdot (e_{fs} - \bar{e}_s)
\;+\; \tilde{\varepsilon}^{\,\mathrm{ext}}_{s} \cdot \bar{e}_s \;\Big]
$$

and $\Omega$ weights

$$
\Omega^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs} = \frac{E_{fs}\,\tilde{\varepsilon}^{\,\mathrm{int}}_{fs}}{\Lambda},
\qquad
\Omega^{\mathrm{ext}}_{s} = \frac{\big(\sum_f E_{fs}\big)\,\tilde{\varepsilon}^{\,\mathrm{ext}}_{s}}{\Lambda}.
$$
